_readme: Region IDs match your real brainData.json exactly. Vascular/network groupings are pedagogical simplifications given lobe-level (not gyral-level) granularity — noted in each 'caveat' field.

mca.name: Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)

syndromes.presentation: Broca's aphasia + contralateral face/arm-predominant weakness (leg relatively spared, since the leg is ACA territory).
Wernicke's aphasia + contralateral superior quadrantanopia; often little to no weakness.
Left hemispatial neglect, left face/arm weakness, anosognosia (denial of deficit).

mca.caveat: MCA territory is broader and more gyrus-specific in reality than lobe-level regions can show — this is a teaching approximation.

aca.name: Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA)

syndromes.presentation: Contralateral leg-predominant weakness (leg/foot motor cortex is on the medial surface, ACA territory), abulia, and gait apraxia if bilateral.

aca.caveat: The leg-predominant weakness pattern relies on the medial motor strip, which this atlas represents at lobe level only.

pca.name: Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA)

syndromes.presentation: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.
Cortical blindness, sometimes with denial of blindness (Anton syndrome).
Central post-stroke pain (Dejerine–Roussy syndrome) — severe contralateral burning pain.

pca.caveat: Thalamic perforators are a small subset of PCA branches; this atlas groups the whole thalamus for simplicity.

vertebrobasilar.name: Vertebrobasilar / PICA System

syndromes.presentation: Crossed sensory loss (ipsilateral face, contralateral body), Horner's syndrome, dysphagia, ipsilateral ataxia.
Ipsilateral ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, scanning speech.

vertebrobasilar.caveat: The brainstem contains many distinct nuclei with different vascular supply; this atlas represents it as one structure.

dmn.name: Default Mode Network
dmn.description: Active during rest, self-referential thought, and mind-wandering; deactivates during externally-focused tasks. Core hubs include medial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate/precuneus.
dmn.clinical_note: DMN connectivity is disrupted in Alzheimer's disease (overlapping with early amyloid deposition sites) and altered in depression (excessive DMN activity linked to rumination).
dmn.caveat: True DMN hubs (mPFC, PCC, precuneus, angular gyrus) are sub-regions of the lobes shown here — this highlights the containing lobes as a teaching approximation, not precise DMN topology.

salience.name: Salience Network
salience.description: Detects behaviorally relevant stimuli and coordinates switching between the Default Mode and Central Executive networks. Core hubs: dorsal anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex.
salience.clinical_note: Salience network dysfunction is implicated in anxiety disorders (hyperresponsivity to threat) and frontotemporal dementia (early insular atrophy).
salience.caveat: dACC is part of the frontal lobe in this atlas's granularity, not a separately modeled structure.

cen.name: Central Executive Network
cen.description: Supports working memory, planning, and goal-directed decision-making. Core hubs: dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and posterior parietal cortex.
cen.clinical_note: CEN engagement is reduced in ADHD and in the depressive rumination state (in favor of DMN dominance).
cen.caveat: dlPFC and posterior parietal cortex are sub-regions of the frontal/parietal lobes shown here, not separately modeled.

memory.label: Memory
memory.summary: Memory isn't stored in one place — it's a system. The hippocampus binds together the different elements of an experience into a coherent memory trace and is essential for forming NEW declarative memories. The amygdala tags memories with emotional significance (why emotionally charged events are remembered more vividly). The thalamus relays sensory information into memory-forming circuits. The prefrontal cortex (frontal lobe) handles working memory — holding and manipulating information moment-to-moment — and retrieval strategy.

language.label: Language
language.summary: Language relies on a left-hemisphere-dominant network (in ~95% of right-handed people). Broca's area plans speech production and grammatical structure. Wernicke's area decodes meaning from spoken/written language. The two are structurally connected by a white matter tract (the arcuate fasciculus), so damage to the connection itself — not just either endpoint — can also cause language deficits (conduction aphasia).

problem_solving.label: Problem-Solving & Executive Function
problem_solving.summary: Problem-solving draws on the Central Executive Network: the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (frontal lobes) for planning, cognitive flexibility, and inhibitory control, working together with the posterior parietal cortex for manipulating information spatially and numerically. The basal ganglia contribute action selection — choosing which response to execute among competing options.

sections.title: CNS vs. PNS
sections.body: The brain and spinal cord are protected by bone (skull and vertebrae respectively) and together form the Central Nervous System (CNS). A key distinguishing feature: CNS tissue does not regenerate after damage — this is why recovery from stroke or TBI plateaus rather than fully reversing. The Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) — all the nerve fibers connecting the CNS to the rest of the body — CAN regrow after damage, a fundamental asymmetry in how these two systems handle injury.

sections.title: Sensory & Motor Pathways
sections.body: Nerve fibers bringing information TO the CNS form sensory pathways, organized by system (vision, hearing, touch, etc.). Nerve fibers carrying commands FROM the CNS to muscles form motor pathways. A critical organizing principle: most sensory and motor pathways are contralateral — information from one side of the body is processed mainly by the opposite hemisphere, and movement on one side of the body is controlled mainly by the opposite hemisphere. This is why a right-hemisphere stroke classically causes left-sided weakness and left visual field neglect.

sections.title: Somatic Nervous System (SNS)
sections.body: The subdivision of the PNS that carries sensory information to the CNS and motor commands to skeletal (voluntary) muscles — everything from reading these words (eye movements) to turning a page. The SNS is under voluntary control.

sections.title: Autonomic Nervous System (ANS)
sections.body: The subdivision of the PNS that controls internal organs largely outside conscious control — heart rate, digestion (stomach contractions), and breathing (diaphragm movement). The ANS further divides into sympathetic (fight-or-flight activation) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) branches, which typically act in opposition to maintain homeostasis.

nervousSystemOverview.caveat: This is foundational neuroanatomical organization, not a substitute for a full neuroanatomy course — treat it as the scaffold that the rest of this atlas's region-specific content sits on top of.

vignettes.text: A 62-year-old presents with intention tremor, dysmetria, and scanning speech, with no weakness on exam.
vignettes.explanation: Coordination deficits without weakness point to the cerebellum — weakness would suggest a corticospinal (pyramidal) lesion instead.

vignettes.text: A patient produces fluent, grammatically well-formed but largely meaningless speech, and cannot follow simple spoken commands.
vignettes.explanation: Fluent but meaningless ('word salad') speech with impaired comprehension is the hallmark of Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia.

vignettes.text: Sudden onset of non-fluent, effortful, telegraphic speech with preserved comprehension, plus right-sided facial and arm weakness.
vignettes.explanation: Non-fluent speech with intact comprehension is classic Broca's aphasia; the co-occurring face/arm weakness reflects the nearby motor strip, both in left MCA superior division territory.

vignettes.text: After bilateral medial temporal lobe surgery, a patient can no longer form new memories, but recalls childhood events normally.
vignettes.explanation: This is the classic H.M. pattern — anterograde amnesia with preserved remote memory points to bilateral hippocampal damage.

vignettes.text: A patient shows a reduced fear response and cannot recognize fear in others' facial expressions, following bilateral temporal lobe calcification.
vignettes.explanation: Selective impairment in fear processing and recognition, with cognition otherwise intact, is the classic bilateral amygdala damage pattern (patient S.M.).

vignettes.text: Following a right-sided stroke, a patient ignores objects and people on their left side and denies anything is wrong.
vignettes.explanation: Left hemispatial neglect with anosognosia localizes to the right posterior parietal cortex.

vignettes.text: After a metal rod pierced the front of the skull, a previously mild-mannered patient becomes impulsive, profane, and unable to hold a job.
vignettes.explanation: This is the Phineas Gage pattern — frontal lobe damage causing profound personality change with relatively preserved basic cognition.

vignettes.text: A patient develops excessive thirst, dilute urine output, and temperature dysregulation after a pituitary-region tumor.
vignettes.explanation: Diabetes insipidus and temperature dysregulation point to hypothalamic involvement, which controls the pituitary/endocrine axis and homeostasis.

vignettes.text: A patient has crossed sensory loss (face on one side, body on the other), drooping eyelid on one side, and difficulty swallowing after a posterior circulation stroke.
vignettes.explanation: This crossed pattern plus Horner's syndrome and dysphagia is classic lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from a brainstem/PICA territory infarct.

vignettes.text: A patient with a strong family history develops involuntary, dance-like movements and progressive cognitive decline in their 40s.
vignettes.explanation: Chorea with a hereditary pattern points to Huntington's disease, a basal ganglia (striatal) degeneration.
